title: Noise, Cognitive Function, and Worker Productivity
research_question: Does noise pollution impair workers' cognitive functions and productivity in low- and middle-income countries, and are workers aware of these effects, influencing their willingness to pay for quiet working conditions?

participants.description: Experiment 1: 128 manual laborers (textile workers) from Nairobi, Kenya, accustomed to factory noise. Experiment 2: 213 individuals from the same population.
participants.recruitment: Recruited from groups of manual laborers gathering at the gates of nearby textile factories hoping to be hired for a day's work.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Engine noise generated by a car engine (used for automechanic training) added to ambient sewing machine noise. Control condition: ambient sewing machine noise (approx. 68.9 dB, like a dishwasher). Treatment condition: ambient + engine noise (approx. 75.6 dB, like a vacuum cleaner). The increase was approximately 7 dB in Experiment 1 and 9.4 dB in Experiment 2.

measures.instrument: Number of pockets sewn, total points earned (quantity + quality), number of pockets meeting various quality criteria (1-6)
Battery of cognitive tests measuring attention, working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and higher-level reasoning. Aggregated into a common factor index.
Key presses on a keyboard (alternating A and B keys for 10 minutes)

measures.construct: Willingness to Pay (WTP) for quiet working conditions
measures.instrument: Modified Becker, DeGroot, and Marschak (BDM) procedure with binary search (KSh0-200)

measures.construct: Beliefs about productivity in quiet vs. noise
measures.instrument: Distribution of 10 beans across 10 bins of possible scores for different compensation schemes and noise levels
Saving/withdrawal decisions (1% daily interest), maize flour purchase (price anomaly), willingness to work additional hour for piece rate
Self-reported annoyance on exit survey (Likert scale 1-10)

findings.consequent: Productivity loss from noise (individual-level treatment effect)

mechanisms: Noise impairs cognitive function (attention, working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, higher-level reasoning), leading to reduced productivity.

Workers' neglect of the productive impact of noise, possibly due to a failure to notice or an awareness of not knowing, prevents them from adjusting their WTP for quiet based on performance incentives.
moderators: Individual ability (high vs. low output workers)
Learning/adaptation over time (early vs. late sessions, early vs. late hours)
Typical noise exposure in daily life
Prompting beliefs about noise impact before WTP elicitation
implementation_implications: Policymakers should take the impact of cognitive impediments like noise seriously, especially in low- and middle-income countries.
Noise pollution can lead to inefficiencies in labor markets due to workers failing to sort into optimal environments or demand appropriate compensation.
Governments should collect comprehensive data on noise exposure.
Regulations on urban noise sources (e.g., car horns) could reduce noise levels without significant efficiency costs.
Raising awareness among workers and firms about the potential effects of noise on productivity could improve outcomes at minimal cost.

limitations: Logistical constraints prevented a sufficiently large sample for long-term adaptation studies, so results may be specific to learning contexts or short-term exposure.
The noise and task combination are specific, limiting generalizability to other types of noise or tasks (e.g., those requiring communication).
The noise levels, while representative, were kept below dangerous levels for ethical reasons, which might affect workers' perceived need to reduce noise.
The study did not directly test the specific model of hierarchical beliefs and inattention, so other explanations for neglect are possible.
The true variance in past-noise exposure among participants might be small, limiting the ability to detect heterogeneity based on typical noise exposure.
The experiment's duration might be too short for workers to form correct beliefs about noise effects on productivity, especially given the randomness of productivity outcomes and end-of-day payments.
